paper_title: GRAPE-Bench: When Vision Degrades, Does Video Reasoning Hold?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.

For example, model that overlooks pedestrian stepping off the curb in heavy rain may report that the crosswalk is clear when the approaching driver needs to yield. Existing video robustness benchmarks use controlled spatiotemporal corruptions to evaluate how models respond as visual conditions deteriorate [1, 21, 73]. Such tests allow systematic comparisons, but the resulting model rankings need not carry over to naturally degraded footage. In Figure 1(a), for example, MiniCPM-V 4.5 outperforms Cosmos-Reason2 on videos with artificially added rain, while their ordering reverses on footage recorded in real rain. Within given video, the choice of questions shapes which capabilities are tested. Video understanding benchmarks use challenging questions to probe how well MLLMs integrate evidence over time [14, 31]. In driving, however, the questions that models find hardest need not be the most relevant to driving decision. In Figure 1(b), models find it harder to count the vehicles initially queued on the left side of the intersection than to determine whether the ego vehicle stopped for red light. Of the two, the traffic signal bears more directly on the decision to stop. This motivates pairing questions at different levels of reasoning demand within the same video, so that an evaluation can probe the limits of models reasoning while still testing the fundamental judgments that matter for safe driving. In this work, we introduce GRAPE-Bench (Graded Robustness Assessment under Perturbed Environments), tiered benchmark for evaluating video understanding under visual degradation  (Table 1)  . The synthetic track applies total of twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos, while the real-world track uses driving footage recorded in rain, snow, or fog, as well as at night. Across both tracks, each video is paired with three independently answerable questions designed to increase in reasoning demand, ranging from fundamental, potentially safety-critical judgments to demanding reasoning stress tests. As summarized in Table 1, GRAPE-Bench jointly covers synthetic and natural degradations, diverse scenarios, and difficultygraded questions, enabling systematic evaluation across visual conditions and reasoning demands. We evaluate 23 open-weight models on both the synthetic and real-world sets, with additional results for proprietary frontier models on the real-world set. In driving scenes, some models outperform their peers under simulated adverse condition but fall behind those same peers on footage recorded under the corresponding natural condition. We also find that some models achieve higher average accuracy across the three tiers despite lower accuracy on questions that test fundamental scene understanding. Their advantage on harder questions can therefore mask weaknesses in basic judgments that matter for safe driving, such as recognizing when vehicle needs to stop or yield. Beyond evaluation, the synthetic set pairs each corrupted video with its clean counterpart, with the same questions for both versions. We use these data to study whether training on synthetic corruptions improves performance under natural degradation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the synthetic set raises Qwen3.5-9Bs accuracy on the realworld set from 76.7% to 81.1%. In the reasoning-enabled setting, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) with privileged access to the clean video during training raises real-world accuracy from 78.1% to 80.4%. The question tiers also let us test whether model can be steered toward fundamental, safety-relevant toward more demanding reasoning tasks. With the underlying VLM frozen, we learn preference-conditioned steering mechanism. On held-out driving videos from both sets, varying the steering coefficient shifts the balance of accuracy between these two types of questions, with little change in overall accuracy. To examine this pattern more broadly, we analyze the 1,716 questions we construct for the real-world driving set of GRAPE-Bench (Section 3.2). We use Claude Opus 5.5 [4] to assign each question an auxiliary safetyrelevance score. As shown in Figure 2, the average ratings decrease from 73.0 at L1 to 64.9 at L2 and 51.5 at L3, with L1 rated higher than L3 in 408 of 572 video groups (71.3%). These observations illustrate why reasoning difficulty alone cannot determine which judgments deserve attention. By evaluating accuracy separately at each level, GRAPE-Bench reveals weaknesses in fundamental, potentially consequential judgments that may otherwise be obscured by overall performance. 3. GRAPE-Bench GRAPE-Bench evaluates video understanding across visual degradation and reasoning difficulty. It contains synthetic set with twelve corruption types applied to daily-life and driving videos, and real-world driving set with naturally occurring rain, snow, nighttime, and fog conditions. Both partitions organize questions into three levels (L1L3), designed to require progressively more demanding reasoning. 3.1. Task Formulation We formulate the task as multiple-choice question answering on visually degraded videos. Given video v, question q, and candidate answer set A, model selects an option and is evaluated against the reference answer y. Each video context is paired with three questions (L1L3), answered independently without answers or rationales from other levels. L1 targets coarse entity or event, L2 focused property, state, action, or relation, and L3 the integration of relevant facts with additional visual evidence. These levels specify intended reasoning demands; their empirical difficulty is assessed through level-wise accuracy. Synthetic samples pair clean video v0 with corrupted counterpart v, keeping questions, options, and reference answers identical. Realworld samples use naturally degraded driving videos. Appendix C.1 details the video input protocol. 3.2. Benchmark Construction Figure 2. Mean safety criticality decreases with difficulty level. We demonstrate that SFT and OPSD on synthetic data improve real-world accuracy, and that lightweight steering vectors control the balance between safety-critical perception and demanding reasoning in frozen model. 2. Motivation Beyond Synthetic Corruptions. Synthetic corruptions provide controlled setting for evaluating visual robustness by perturbing video inputs while preserving their underlying content and questions. Existing benchmarks, including MVTamperBench, PVRBench, and DriveBench, have adopted such perturbations to probe model reliability [1, 21, 73]  (Table 1)  . However, relative model performance under synthetic perturbations need not persist under naturally adverse conditions. We observe ranking reversal in GRAPE-Bench: MiniCPM-V 4.5-8B outperforms Cosmos-Reason2-8B across all four synthetic driving corruptions, yet their ranking reverses under each corresponding real-world condition (Tables 2 and 3). Figure 1(a) further illustrates this discrepancy by juxtaposing representative synthetic and real-world rain footage with model rankings based on aggregate accuracy over the corresponding evaluation subsets. These rank reversals motivate evaluating models under both controlled corruptions and naturally adverse driving conditions. Difficulty vs. Safety Relevance. Perception Test, TempCompass, MotionBench, and TOMATO probe specific perceptual, motion, and temporal skills [25, 34, 43, 58]. VCR-Bench and MINERVA analyze annotated reasoning traces [39, 44], while VideoReasonBench probes increasingly difficult tasks involving observations, latent states, and future predictions [35]. More recently, VideoMME-v2 introduces capability hierarchies to assess consistency across related queries and reasoning sequences [16]. GRAPE-Bench extends these evaluations to visual degradation, examining performance across question levels under synthetic and natural adverse conditions. Robustness of Multimodal Models. Multimodal robustness depends on visual input quality and reasoning over degraded evidence [21, 46, 62]. At the image level, RBench studies acquisition and processing distortions [30], while MLLM-IC evaluates corruption types and severity levels [46]. Video benchmarks examine spatial and temporal tampering in MVTamperBench [1], and answer accuracy and reasoning under synthetic disturbances in PVRBench [21]. On the method side, Robust-R1 employs degradation-aware reasoning and reward-driven alignment [62], while Robust-U1 combines visual self-recovery with reasoning over corrupted and recovered images [63]. More recently, ROVA encourages consistency between clean and corrupted videos [21]. GRAPE-Bench complements these efforts with graded questions across synthetic corruptions and naturally adverse conditions, probing video reasoning robustness at different difficulty levels. Driving Benchmarks under Adverse Conditions. Driving benchmarks connect visual understanding with prediction and decision-making. LingoQA and nuScenes-QA evaluate driving scene understanding through QA [38, 45], while DriveLM organizes perception, prediction, and planning questions as graph [59]. DriveXQA uses multiple sensor modalities for question answering in adverse driving scenes [64]. DriveBench evaluates driving VLMs under clean, corrupted, and text-only inputs, revealing limitations in visual grounding [73]. ObsDriveBench studies naturally adverse weather using camera, LiDAR, and radar observations, assessing observability awareness, spatial reliability, and risk-aware decisions [75]. PaSBench-Video evaluates proactive safety warnings in streaming video across including driving [84]. Unlike these several domains, capability-oriented decompositions, GRAPE-Bench introduces human-annotated real-world driving-video set with three difficulty-graded questions per video. Combined with its synthetic daily-life and driving sets, it enables robustness evaluation across visual conditions and reasoning demands while distinguishing difficulty from safety relevance. The endpoint trade-off is consistent across domains, although intermediate settings do not yield strictly monotonic changes. Finding 4. Preference steering shifts the balance between safety-relevant judgments and demanding reasoning with little change in overall accuracy. 6. Related Work Video Understanding Benchmarks. Video understanding benchmarks have progressed from broad capability assessment to structured reasoning evaluation [14, 31, 39]. NExT-QA and STAR examine causal, temporal, and situated reasoning [68, 71], while broader suites cover more 8 7. Conclusion We introduced GRAPE-Bench to study video reasoning under synthetic and natural visual degradation through three questions of increasing reasoning demand per video. Model rankings can reverse between simulated and real-world driving conditions, yet training on the synthetic set improves Qwen3.5-9Bs accuracy on real-world footage. We observe this transfer with supervised fine-tuning and, when reasoning is enabled, with on-policy self-distillation from teacher given access to the clean video. The question tiers reveal that model with higher overall accuracy can still be less reliable on basic judgments that matter for safe driving. Using two learned steering vectors, we can adjust frozen models balance of accuracy between these judgments and more demanding questions, with little change in overall accuracy. These findings highlight the value of testing even simple judgments under naturally adverse conditions when driving decision depends on them.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: In this supplementary material, we provide additional details on benchmark construction, evaluation, and syntheticto-real training, expand the related-work discussion and our contributions, and discuss limitations and societal impact. The material is organized as follows: Section describes synthetic question verification and corruption generation. Section covers real-world clip preparation, question annotation, and metadata. Section presents evaluation details, paired corruption analyses, and additional model comparisons. Section provides training recipes, distillation objectives, and additional transfer analyses. Section reviews additional related work and explains our distinct contributions. Section discusses limitations, potential benefits, and risks of downstream use. A. Synthetic Set Construction A.1. Automatic Question Verification Shared verification gates. The pipeline implements six shared gates. G0 (option sanity) checks the option count, nonempty and nonduplicate option text, and consistency between the answer label and the available options. G1 (logic and hierarchy) checks that questions are self-contained, follow common visual thread, and satisfy the intended hierarchy. G2 (diversity) checks for near-paraphrases across levels and, under the embedding-based configuration, repeated L1 questions within the same subcategory. G3 (visual grounding and visual-only wording) comprises two checks: G3a screens references to narration, audio, or external subtitles, while G3b checks the stated answers against sampled video frames without transcript. G4 (video necessity) tests whether question can be answered from prior knowledge alone, using text-only response produced without the video or answer options. G5 (distractor plausibility) checks that options are of the same semantic kind and remain plausible without viewing the video. Execution and difficulty audit. G1 and G3a precede distractor generation. The subsequent checks run in the order G0, G3b, G4, G5, and G2. An additional difficulty audit (GD) is configured before G2 for EgoSchema, NExT-QA, STAR, and VRU-Accident. It assesses the intended difficulty progression from the final questions, options, and frames without construction metadata or reference answers. Revision and inclusion. When check flags malformed answer options, inconsistent option formats, or weak distractors, the pipeline regenerates the options at the affected question levels and reruns verification. If the group still fails, or if the failure requires changes to the questions, the pipeline re-extracts visual facts from the sampled frames and uses them to regenerate the full L1L3 question group. It reuses the original frames by default and samples new frames when the verifier requests more visual evidence. As reported in Section 3.3, 10,818 groups passed automatic verification. We manually reviewed, revised, and approved the remaining 23 groups for release. The metadata record the original automatic verification outcome. A.2. Synthetic Corruptions Corruption set and assignment. We use twelve corruption types to cover adverse weather, lens and glass degradation, exposure changes, blur, and compression or transmission artifacts. Rain, snow, nighttime, and fog are assigned to the 3,000 question groups from VRU-Accident. The remaining eight types, including wet lens, glass occlusion, overexposure, underexposure, defocus blur, motion blur, lowbitrate compression, and bitstream errors, are assigned to the 7,841 groups from NExT-QA, STAR, EgoSchema, and Video-MME short/medium. The benchmark uses one fixed parameter configuration for each corruption type. Each question group receives one corrupted video shared by its three question levels, while its questions, answer options, and reference answers remain unchanged. Assignments are balanced within each source-dataset pool, and groups derived from the same source video receive different corruption types. The weather and general-corruption subsets therefore cover different source content rather than fully crossed video-by-corruption design. Corruption implementation. Rain, snow, and nighttime are generated with procedural renderer operating in linearlight space. Rain and snow use multiple particle layers with temporally coherent trajectories, combined with illumination changes and haze. Rain additionally approximates wetroad reflections, whereas snow represents airborne flakes rather than accumulated ground snow. Nighttime combines reduced ambient illumination with approximate headlights, street lighting, glare, and signal-dependent noise. These effects use heuristic scene assumptions rather than reconstructed scene geometry. Fog is generated separately using smoothly varying, drifting opacity fields and contrast atten1 uation. Wet-lens corruption adapts the droplet-refraction effect provided in HiKER-SGG [82]. Fixed, multi-scale droplet fields spatially remap each input frame, producing persistent lens-attached distortions rather than overlaying unrelated scene content. Glass occlusion combines soft-edged translucent masks, local blur, and tint to approximate obscured glass. Defocus uses Gaussian blur, while motion blur integrates neighboring frames under simulated camera shake to produce temporal trails. Overexposure and underexposure use intensity scaling and nonlinear tone mapping, with clipping in the overexposed case. Low-bitrate corruption uses constrained H.264 encoding through FFmpeg. Following prior work on video corruption robustness [77], we introduce bitstream errors directly into encoded video data rather than drawing image-space blocks. The damaged stream is decoded and re-encoded into valid video, preserving visible decoding artifacts for consistent playback. We will release the code so readers can inspect how each corruption is applied and which parameters it uses. B. Real-World Set Construction B.1. Video Sources and Preparation We collect real-world driving footage from DrivingDojo [67], Boreas [8], Boreas-RT [33], BDD100K [78], and DrivingHazy/GoProHazy [12]. Candidate clips are identified using available weather and time-of-day metadata and screened for suitability for question annotation. We reconstruct DrivingDojo videos from the provided image sequences, extract 15-second clips from continuous Boreas and Boreas-RT recordings, and retain up to the first 30 seconds of each BDD100K and DrivingHazy/GoProHazy video. Shorter videos retain their full temporal extent. All clips are prepared at 5 fps without adding synthetic weather effects. DrivingDojo clips retain their source resolution of 1920 1080, while clips from the other sources are prepared at width of 1280 pixels with their aspect ratios preserved. Real-world atmospheric haze in DrivingHazy and GoProHazy is included in the fog category for analysis. B.2. Question Design and Annotation Expert annotators developed the real-world questions, writing some directly and using AI-generated drafts as starting point for others. They inspected each clip using playback and frame stepping and excluded unsuitable clips. For each retained clip, the annotators finalized three self-contained questions, one per difficulty level, after checking each question, its four options, and its reference answer against the video and revising or replacing questions as needed. Looking across the completed real-world set, we observed the following broad patterns in what questions at each difficulty level ask: L1 questions often ask about salient entity, event, or scene state, such as whether pedestrian is present or nearby vehicle is moving. L2 questions often concern specific attribute, spatial relation, or change over time, such as how another vehicle moves relative to the ego vehicle or how the lane layout changes during maneuver. L3 questions often combine several observations, for example asking how many vehicles passed and in what order. Questions share the visual context but are answered independently, without reference answers from other levels. Figure 7 shows the words that characterize each level. Temporal annotations. prepared driving clip may contain multiple events and road users. We therefore allow annotators to specify question-specific observation endpoint when constructing questions and reference answers. This allows annotators to control the amount and temporal scope of evidence relevant to each question, helping align its evidence demands with the intended question level. For example, shorter prefix can reduce ambiguity about the target entity or event in an L1 question, while specified observation endpoint can support prediction about subsequent events. C.3. Accuracy across Difficulty Levels Empirical accuracy need not follow strict level ordering. On the real-world set, 23 of the 24 open-weight configurations exhibit L1 > L2 > L3 in aggregate accuracy  (Table 3)  . Kimi K3 is the exception, scoring higher at L2 than at L1 (88.8% vs. 86.7%), although L3 remains the lowest-scoring level for all 24 configurations. Local reversals also occur: under real fog, 11 of these configurations score higher at L3 than at L2. For example, Qwen3.5-27B achieves 92.0% at L3 compared with 88.0% at L2. The levels describe intended reasoning demands without imposing universal empirical accuracy ordering. These comparisons alone cannot explain whether reversals arise from model behavior, the question mix, or annotation difficulty; resolving this requires auditing individual questions. C.4. GPT5.6 Sol leads overall (87.8%), but its advantage over the strongest open-weight model, Kimi K3 (85.4%), varies from 1.0 point in fog to 3.7 points in snow. The advantage also differs across question levels: 3.5 points at L1, 1.0 at L2, and 2.6 at L3. Its overall lead therefore combines uneven gains across conditions and reasoning demands. All six proprietary configurations score lower at L3 than at both L1 and L2; even GPT-5.6 Sol reaches 83.4% at L3, compared with 90.2% at L1. Data Splits and Adaptation Data and splits. For the transfer experiments in Section 4, all training uses the synthetic set. We split its 10,841 chains by source video and hold out 5% (533 chains, 1,599 questions). The remaining 10,308 chains (30,924 questions) form the training partition; each L1, L2, and L3 question of chain is one training sample. The held-out chains are divided into validation split (299 chains, 897 questions), used for hyperparameter and variant selection, and test split (234 chains, 702 questions), used only for reporting. The training, validation, and test splits are mutually disjoint by source video. The main transfer comparisons use the final checkpoint of each training run. For these transfer experiments, the real-world set (572 videos, 1,716 questions) is used exclusively for testing: no real-world video, question, or label enters training, model selection, or hyperparameter tuning.

sections.title: Contributions
sections.content: E.1. Video Understanding and Reasoning Evaluation benchmarks. Video benchmarks span broad capability assessment and detailed reasoning evaluation [14, 31, 39]. NExT-QA and STAR emphasize temporal, causal, and situated reasoning [68, 71]; MVBench, VideoMME, and EgoSchema broaden task, domain, and temporal coverage [14, 31, 37]. VCR-Bench and MINERVA include reasoning traces [39, 44], while VideoReasonBench and Video-MME-v2 further structure reasoning and capability evaluation [16, 35]. Sensitivity studies also examine how video-language models answer when temporal or visual evidence is altered [19, 61]. GRAPE-Bench examines 7 how degradation affects performance across question levels and how intended difficulty relates to safety relevance. Video reasoning models. LLaVA-Video expands video instruction tuning through generated captioning and QA data [83]. Qwen3-VL advances long-context understanding and temporal alignment [6], while InternVL3.5 improves multimodal reasoning through reinforcement learning [66]. Apollo studies design choices for video input and model architectures [88]. Video-R1 and VideoChatR1 reinforce temporal reasoning and spatiotemporal perception [13, 32], while VideoChat-R1.5 increases perceptual computation through iterative inspection of spatiotemporal regions [76]. Such advances motivate testing whether stronger reasoning remains reliable when visual evidence degrades. Our conditionand level-specific evaluations reveal whether aggregate improvements extend to fundamental, safety-relevant judgments. E.2. Robustness and Adverse Driving Conditions Controlled visual degradations. ImageNet-C systematized common-corruption evaluation [22], with subsequent work extending robustness analysis to spatiotemporal and video-language models [56, 57, 77]. R-Bench and MLLM-IC examine image distortions and fine-grained multimodal capabilities [30, 46]; MVTamperBench and tampering and perturbed PVRBench evaluate temporal video reasoning [1, 21]. Robust-R1, Robust-U1, and ROVA explore degradation-aware reasoning, visual recovery, and clean-to-corrupted consistency [21, 62, 63]. GRAPE-Bench combines paired clean-to-corrupted comparisons with natural-video evaluation, distinguishing controlled corruption losses from performance under realworld conditions. Naturally adverse driving conditions. ACDC, Boreas, and Seeing Through Fog provide observations under adverse weather or across seasons [7, 8, 54]. SHIFT supplies controlled synthetic domain shifts [60], and driving perception benchmarks isolate corruptions in LiDAR, camera-based birds-eye-view inputs, or multiple sensor streams [20, 29, 74]. DriveLM and DriveVLM connect visual reasoning with perception or planning tasks [59, 65], and DriveBench tests reliability under clean, corrupted, and text-only inputs [73]. ObsDriveBench studies observability, spatial reliability, and risk-aware decisions using camera, LiDAR, and radar observations in adverse weather [75]. Our real-world partition focuses on video QA using the available video prefix. Its three-level design and auxiliary safety-relevance ratings support analysis of both reasoning demands and the significance of the judgments affected. E.3. Adaptation and Preference Control Synthetic supervision and distillation. Generated instruction data [83] and filtered rationales [80] support multimodal and reasoning supervision. Earlier approaches use teacher predictions for distillation, train students on augmented inputs with teacher labels, or encourage consistency across augmentations [23, 24, 72]. Our synthetic corruptions provide clean counterpart to each degraded input for teacher supervision. Imitation learning addresses distribution mismatch by collecting feedback on states visited by the learner [53]. Similarly, on-policy distillation uses teacher feedback on student-generated responses [2]. We adapt this principle by having frozen clean-video teacher score the students corrupted-input reasoning trajectories. Comparing this recipe with direct and reasoning-based SFT tests whether the synthetic partition supports transfer to naturally degraded videos. Preference-conditioned steering. DPO optimizes preference pairs [51]; MODPO and Panacea address multiple objectives and varying preferences [85, 87]; and BiPO learns representation-level steering vectors [9]. Other methods control preferences with attribute conditioning or interpolate models optimized for different rewards [11, 52]. We draw on these ideas to control an accuracy trade-off exposed by the benchmark. Two learned vectors define shared intervention and preference-dependent direction in frozen VLM, shifting emphasis between basic judgments and demanding reasoning. Separate synthetic and real-world experiments evaluate held-out control, reporting overall accuracy alongside level-specific changes. E.4. Our Unique Contributions Which judgments hold up when vision degrades? PVRBench tests reasoning under controlled video perturbations [21], ObsDriveBench studies perception and risk under naturally adverse driving conditions [75], and VideoReasonBench probes different levels of reasoning [35]. GRAPE-Bench brings these questions into one evaluation. Each video has three independently answerable questions of increasing reasoning demand, both on the synthetic set spanning twelve corruptions across daily-life and driving videos and on driving footage recorded in rain, snow, fog, or at night. We then used Claude Opus 5.5 to rate the safety relevance of the completed real-world questions. L1 questions received the highest ratings on average. For example, recognizing whether car stopped for red light can matter more to driving decision than counting the vehicles queued beside it. What does an overall score conceal? We evaluate 23 open-weight models across both sets and additional proprietary frontier models on real-world footage. Models can reverse rank between simulated rain and real rain. Rankings also depend on which judgments are scored. On realworld videos, Kimi K3 leads Qwen3.8-Flash-Next overall but trails it on L1. Larger models generally perform better, although scaling alone does not guarantee higher real-world 8 also hide failures affecting underrepresented groups, motivating broader data collection and subgroup evaluation. More robust video understanding could support intrusive surveillance, while steering could be used to improve selected metrics at the expense of unreported capabilities. Transparent reporting across conditions and difficulty levels is therefore important when interpreting or reusing these methods. accuracy or smaller losses under corruption. Can training improve or steer these judgments? Paired clean and corrupted videos let us test whether synthetic supervision transfers to real driving footage. Direct SFT raises Qwen3.5-9Bs real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, although better fit to synthetic data can hurt transfer. Building on on-policy distillation [2], we give the teacher the clean video and have it score reasoning steps produced by the student on the corrupted video. This raises real-world accuracy from 78.1% with reasoning SFT to 80.4%. Building on representation steering [9], we also learn two vectors for the frozen Qwen3.5-9B and vary single coefficient to shift accuracy between basic, safety-relevant judgments and more demanding reasoning. We observe this trade-off on held-out videos in both domains, using vectors trained separately in each, with little change in overall accuracy. F. Limitations and Societal Impact F.1. Limitations Corruption severity. We evaluate each synthetic corruption at single intensity. We will release code for adjusting the severity of each corruption so that researchers can render the same clips at several intensities. Holding the clips and questions fixed would make it possible to measure how rapidly accuracy declines with severity at each question level. Inference efficiency. Our evaluation focuses on answer accuracy under visual degradation. Driving systems must also make decisions in real time, so the time model takes to answer matters alongside its accuracy. Measuring end-to-end latency and peak memory on the same hardware would help identify open-weight models that maintain accuracy within given response time and memory budget. F.2. Societal Impact Potential benefits and deployment limits. By exposing failures under degraded visual evidence and separating performance across difficulty levels, GRAPE-Bench may help researchers identify weaknesses that aggregate scores conceal. Synthetic training and lightweight steering provide tools for studying how to address these weaknesses. However, improved benchmark accuracy or preference for L1 questions does not establish safer driving behavior. Deployment decisions require evaluation of actual task outcomes, uncertainty, and failure handling under relevant operating conditions; the benchmark is research instrument rather than safety certification. Privacy, representation, and misuse. Source videos can contain identifiable people, vehicles, and locations.
